newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court finds Belgium's student tideover allowances biased.
newsitem.headline: Court finds Belgium's student tideover allowances biased.

text.p: The European Court of Justice ruled on Thursday the European Commission can challenge national provisions which indirectly discriminate against migrant workers without proving actual discrimination.

The court did not require the Commission to submit statistical data but said "it must be borne in mind that a provision of national law must be regarded as indirectly discriminatory if it is intrinsically liable to affect migrant workers more than national workers...and it is not necessary to find the provision in question does in practice affect a substantially higher proportion of migrant workers. It is sufficient that it is liable to have such an effect."

Belgium's system of offering "tideover allowances" to recent graduates of Belgian secondary schools was ruled a violation of freedom of movement provisions of the EU Treaty. "To impose on the children of migrant workers the obligation to complete their studies in Belgium is tantamount to imposing a condition of prior residence condemned by the court in prior rulings," the court said.

The court tossed out a Commission challenge to Belgium's practice of encouraging employers to take on beneficiaries of tideover allowances by offering to assume responsibility for social security contributions of those wholly unemployed and on benefit.

The court reasoned that Community rules on freedom of movement for workers as applied to unemployment insurance do not cover young people seeking first employment, but may only be evoked by someone previously holding the status of worker.

"Failure of a member state to fulfil its obligations - Indirect discrimination on grounds of nationality - Children of migrant workers - Social advantages - Young people seeking first employment - Access to special employment programmes"
Commission of the European Communities, applicant

application for a declaration that by requiring that young people seeking their first employment have completed their secondary education in an establishment subsidized or approved by the Belgian state (or by one of its communities) in order to be eligible for tidever allowances, and by encouraging employers at the same time to take on beneficiaries of those unemployment allowances by providing for the state to assume responsibility in such a case for the remuneration and social security contributions for such workers if they are wholly unemployed and on benefit, the Kingdom of Belgium has failed to fulfil its obligatons under article 48 of the EC Treaty and artices 3 and 7 of regulation (EEC) No 1612/68 of the Council of 15 October 1968 on freedom of movement for workers within the Community (OJ, English Special Edition 1968 (II), p. 475),

1. Declares that by requiring that dependent children of migrant workers of the Community residing in Belgium have completed their secondary education in an establishment subsidized or approved by the Belgian state or by one of its communities in order to be eligible for tidever allowances, the Kingdom of Belgium has failed to fulfil its obligatons under article 48 of the EC Treaty and artices 3 and 7 of regulation (EEC) No 1612/68 of the Council of 15 October 1968 on freedom of movement for workers within the Community;
2. Dismisses the remainder of the application;
3. Orders the parties to bear their own costs.
